lessons.title: Set up Cursor and get fast with Tab autocomplete
lessons.summary: Install Cursor, open a real project, and learn to read multi-edit Tab suggestions before accepting them instead of typing every change by hand.
lessons.goal: Install Cursor, open a real project in it, and complete a small multi-site edit using Tab to accept predicted follow-on edits instead of typing each one by hand.
lessons.whyItMatters: Tab is Cursor's headline feature and the one you'll use every minute you're coding — unlike plain autocomplete, it predicts your next several edits across a file, not just the next few tokens, and lets you jump between predicted edit sites with Tab. Getting comfortable reading a suggestion before accepting it, on day one, is what separates fast disciplined use from carelessly accepting a subtly wrong edit.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Cursor installed (cursor.com) on macOS, Windows, or Linux, and a real project you already know open in it — not a brand-new empty repo, since you need to be able to judge suggestion quality. The free Hobby tier is enough for this lesson.
steps: Download and install Cursor from cursor.com and open it.
Open a project folder you already know well (File → Open Folder), so you can judge whether suggestions are actually correct.
Open a file with a repeated pattern — a component with matching prop names, or a function/variable used in several places.
Start typing a small, real change (rename a variable, add a parameter) and watch for the gray 'ghost' suggestion.
Read the full suggestion before accepting — Tab predicts your next several edits, so it may jump ahead to another location in the file, not just complete the current line.
Press Tab to accept and jump to the next predicted edit site; press Esc to reject a suggestion that's wrong.
Make one deliberate multi-site edit (e.g. rename a variable used four times) and use Tab repeatedly, checking each predicted follow-on edit before accepting it.
Save the file and run `git diff` to confirm only the edits you actually intended were made.
lessons.prompt: This lesson doesn't use a chat prompt — Tab works as you type, not from an instruction. Use this hands-on practice task instead: rename the variable `usr` to `user` everywhere it appears in the current file, including any function parameter and every usage that also referenced it. Type the first rename yourself, then let Tab handle the rest as it detects the same edit is needed elsewhere in the file.
lessons.explanation: Tab's prediction model looks at the edit you just made and proposes what it thinks logically follows — sometimes at a different location in the file, which is why accepting a suggestion can jump your cursor instead of just completing a token. Reading the full suggestion before accepting matters because a plausible-looking prediction isn't automatically correct — it might extend a rename to a similarly-named but unrelated variable. Practicing on a project you already know lets you judge suggestion quality directly instead of trusting output you can't yet evaluate.
lessons.example: A developer opens a file with a function `calculateTotal(items, taxRate)` used in three places. They start renaming `taxRate` to `taxPercent` at the definition. Tab immediately suggests the matching edit at each of the three call sites — the developer presses Tab three times, reading each suggested change before accepting, and presses Esc once where the suggestion incorrectly also flagged an unrelated `taxRate` variable in a different function.
lessons.exercise: In your own Cursor install, open a real project you know well. Find a small, real edit that touches the same identifier or pattern in three or more places — a rename, an added parameter, a repeated formatting fix. Make the first edit by hand, then use Tab to step through and deliberately accept or reject each subsequent suggestion.
lessons.expectedResult: Cursor's Tab correctly predicts and offers to apply the same or related edit at other locations in the file after your first manual edit, and you can point to at least one suggestion you rejected because it was wrong.
commonMistakes: Accepting every Tab suggestion reflexively without reading it, especially when it jumps to an unfamiliar part of the file.
Practicing on unfamiliar code where you can't judge whether a correct-looking suggestion is actually right.
Expecting Tab to understand intent from nothing — it predicts from an edit pattern you start, not from a description.
lessons.proTip: If Tab keeps proposing something you don't want in a specific pattern (a semicolon style you don't use, a naming convention that's wrong for this project), that's a signal for a Rules file, covered in a later lesson, rather than fighting it suggestion by suggestion — Tab respects the same project conventions once they're documented.

lessons.title: Chat with your codebase to understand it before changing anything
lessons.summary: Use Cursor's Chat panel with @-mentions and codebase indexing to get an accurate, citable map of an unfamiliar project before making any edits.
lessons.goal: Get an accurate, citable explanation of an unfamiliar codebase's structure and one real flow through it, using Cursor Chat.
lessons.whyItMatters: Cursor indexes your codebase for semantic search, so Chat can answer real questions about how the actual code works instead of guessing from a generic pattern. Most professional use of an AI code editor starts inside someone else's code — a client project, an inherited codebase, an open-source dependency — and asking for an accurate map before editing prevents changes based on a wrong mental model.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A real project open in Cursor, ideally one that's new to you. Let Cursor finish indexing the codebase (a status indicator appears while indexing runs) before asking detailed questions.
steps: Open the Chat panel (Cmd+L on Mac, Ctrl+L on Windows/Linux) rather than inline edit — you want an answer first, not a change.
Wait for codebase indexing to complete so Chat can search semantically across the whole project, not just the open file.
Ask for a high-level tour: what the project does, its entry points, and its top-level structure.
Use @ to explicitly mention specific files or folders (e.g. @src/api) when you want the answer grounded in exactly those files.
Ask Chat to trace one real, specific flow through the code end to end, citing file paths and function names in order.
Ask which command actually runs the test suite and how the project builds.
Open at least two of the cited files yourself to verify the explanation is accurate before trusting the rest.
Keep this as a read-only conversation — don't let it drift into asking for edits in the same thread until you've verified the explanation.
lessons.prompt: Using only what's in this codebase (@[paste folder or key files]), give me: 1) a one-paragraph summary of what this project does, 2) the main entry point file(s) with exact paths, 3) the top-level folder structure and what each major folder is for, 4) a step-by-step trace of what happens when [describe one real flow, e.g. 'a user submits the signup form'], citing the specific files and functions involved in order, 5) the exact command to run the test suite. If you're not confident about something, say so instead of guessing.
lessons.explanation: Explicitly @-mentioning files or folders grounds the answer in Cursor's semantic index of your actual code rather than a plausible-sounding generic explanation, and asking for a specific real flow traced with cited file paths gives you something directly checkable — you can open exactly those files and confirm. The 'say so if not confident' instruction reduces the risk of a fluent, wrong answer about the part of the codebase Chat is least sure about, since indexing quality can vary in very large or unusual repos.
lessons.example: A developer joins a project with an unfamiliar checkout flow in a mid-size e-commerce codebase. In Chat, they mention @src/checkout and ask for a trace of what happens from 'add to cart' through order confirmation. Cursor's response cites the client component handling the click, the API route it calls, the database write, and the confirmation email trigger, each with an exact path. The developer opens two of the cited files and confirms the explanation matches the actual code before trusting the rest.
lessons.exercise: Open a real, unfamiliar (to you) project in your own Cursor account. Use the prompt above with an @-mention of the relevant folder, get the tour and one traced flow, and open at least two of the cited files yourself to check accuracy.
lessons.expectedResult: A structured explanation with specific file paths you can verify, an accurate trace of one real flow through the code, the correct test command, and an honest flag on anything Chat wasn't confident about.
commonMistakes: Asking broad architecture questions before indexing has finished, getting a thinner or stale answer.
Skipping the @-mention and getting a more generic answer than the codebase actually supports.
Trusting the explanation without opening any cited file to verify it.
lessons.proTip: If you'll come back to this codebase repeatedly, save the verified tour somewhere durable — a README section, a wiki page, or later a Rules/AGENTS.md file — instead of re-deriving it in a new Chat thread every time.

lessons.title: Make precise inline edits and coordinated multi-file changes
lessons.summary: Use Cmd+K inline edit for surgical single-location changes and multi-file agent edits for changes that span several files, reviewing each diff before accepting.
lessons.goal: Correctly choose between inline edit (Cmd+K) for a precise, local change and a multi-file edit for a change that spans several files, reviewing the diff before accepting either.
lessons.whyItMatters: Cursor gives you two different edit tools for a reason: inline edit is fast and scoped to exactly the selection or file you're looking at, while multi-file edits (the old 'Composer' surface, now part of Agent) coordinate a change across many files at once. Picking the wrong one either wastes a full agent run on a one-line fix or forces you to manually repeat a coordinated change across files by hand.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A real project open in Cursor with at least one change you want that touches two or more related files — a renamed function used by its callers, or a shared type plus its usages.
steps: For a small, local, well-understood change, select the relevant code and use inline edit (Cmd+K) with a specific instruction.
Review the inline diff shown directly in the editor before accepting — it previews the change in place.
For a change that spans multiple files (a shared interface plus its call sites, a renamed export plus imports), open the multi-file edit view instead of doing each file separately with inline edit.
Describe the full scope of the multi-file change up front, naming the files or pattern involved if you know them.
Review the proposed diff file by file, not just the summary, before accepting.
Accept or reject changes per file — you don't have to accept the whole batch as one unit.
If one file's proposed change is wrong, reject just that file and give a targeted correction instead of restarting the whole task.
Run your build or tests after accepting to confirm the coordinated change is actually consistent across files.
lessons.prompt:
Inline edit (Cmd+K) example — select the function signature first: "Add an optional `locale` parameter defaulting to 'en', and use it to format the returned date string instead of the hardcoded format."

Multi-file edit example — no selection needed: "Rename the exported type `UserRecord` to `UserProfile` everywhere it is defined, imported, or used across the project. Do not change its shape or fields, only the name. List every file you touched when done."
lessons.explanation: Inline edit works on a selection or the current file only, so an instruction as specific as 'add this parameter and use it here' produces a tightly scoped diff you can read at a glance. The multi-file prompt explicitly states the boundary of the change (only the name, not the shape) and asks for a list of touched files, turning the result into something reviewable file by file rather than a diff you have to reverse-engineer to understand scope. Reviewing per file, and rejecting just the wrong ones, keeps a mostly-correct multi-file change from being thrown out entirely over one bad edit.
lessons.example: A developer needs to rename a shared TypeScript type used in 11 files. Doing this with inline edit file by file would take 11 separate reviews; instead they describe the full rename as one multi-file task. Cursor proposes changes across all 11 files; the developer reviews each diff, accepts 10, and rejects one file where the edit had also incorrectly renamed an unrelated local variable that happened to share the old name — then sends a one-line correction for just that file.
lessons.exercise: Pick one small local change and use inline edit (Cmd+K) for it. Then pick one real change in your own project that touches at least two related files, and run it as a multi-file edit, reviewing and accepting or rejecting the diff file by file.
lessons.expectedResult: The inline edit produces a tightly scoped, easily reviewed change to exactly the selected code. The multi-file edit produces a diff broken down by file that you can accept or reject individually, with the overall change consistent enough that your build or tests still pass afterward.
commonMistakes: Using multi-file edits for a one-line fix that inline edit would have handled faster and with a smaller diff to review.
Accepting a whole multi-file batch without reviewing individual files, missing one incorrect edit hidden among several correct ones.
Not naming the exact boundary of a multi-file change ('only the name, not the shape'), leading to scope creep into unrelated code.
lessons.proTip: For a multi-file change with a hard boundary ('never touch files under src/legacy/'), say the exclusion explicitly in the prompt — but if you find yourself repeating the same exclusion across many tasks, that's a sign it belongs in a Rules file instead, covered next.

lessons.title: Delegate a whole task to Agent mode, with review checkpoints
lessons.summary: Describe a bounded feature or fix to Cursor's Agent, let it plan, edit across files, run terminal commands and tests, and review its work before accepting.
lessons.goal: Have Cursor's Agent complete a real, bounded task end to end — editing multiple files, running commands, and iterating on its own errors — while you review before merging.
lessons.whyItMatters: Agent mode is Cursor's core 'describe a task, get a working change' workflow: it plans, edits across files, runs terminal commands and tests, and fixes its own errors until the task is done. That autonomy is exactly what makes it valuable and exactly what makes an unreviewed accept risky — the skill is running the loop with real checkpoints, not disabling your judgment.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A real project with a runnable build/test command, and one bounded task in mind (a small feature, a well-described bug). Model choice is available in the Agent panel — Auto is fine to start.
steps: Open the Agent view (Cmd+I) and describe the task as a spec: goal, constraints, and what 'done' looks like.
Choose a model deliberately for anything non-trivial — Auto for routine tasks, a flagship model (Claude Opus, GPT-5.5, or Cursor's own Composer) for architecture-sensitive work.
Let Agent propose a plan or start working; watch for it running terminal commands (installing dependencies, running tests) as part of the loop.
Interrupt if it heads in the wrong direction early — redirecting mid-task is cheaper than reviewing a finished wrong diff.
When it reports done, review the diff file by file, not just the summary.
Explicitly ask it to run the test suite and show the real output if it hasn't already.
Accept the files that are correct; reject and give a targeted correction for any that aren't.
Commit only once the diff and real test output both check out.
lessons.prompt:
Task: Add input validation to the newsletter signup form.

Goal: reject invalid emails client-side before submission and show an inline error.

Acceptance criteria:
- Submitting an empty or malformed email shows the message "Enter a valid email address" under the field, without a page reload.
- A valid email submits normally, unchanged from current behavior.
- No new dependency is added — use a plain regex check consistent with validation already used elsewhere in this form (check for an existing pattern first).

Constraints: only touch the signup form component and its existing validation utility, if one exists. Do not change the submission API.

Definition of done: existing tests still pass, and a new test covers both the invalid and valid email cases.

Run the actual test command when you're done and show me the output, not a summary.
lessons.explanation: Structuring the task as a spec — goal, acceptance criteria, constraints, and a definition of done — gives Agent enough to plan correctly on the first pass instead of guessing at scope, which matters more here than in a one-shot inline edit because Agent may touch several files and run commands unsupervised for longer stretches. Asking it to check for an existing validation pattern before adding new logic prevents duplicate, inconsistent approaches. Requiring real pasted test output, not a claim, closes the gap between 'Agent says it works' and 'it demonstrably works.'
lessons.example: A developer gives Agent the newsletter validation spec above. Agent finds an existing `isValidEmail` utility already used in another form, reuses it instead of writing new regex, edits the signup component, adds one test file, runs the test command, and reports 14 passing tests including two new ones. The developer reviews the 22-line diff, confirms the reused utility rather than duplicated logic, and merges.
lessons.exercise: Pick one real, small, bounded task in your own project — a validation rule, a small feature, a described bug. Write it as a spec using the template above, run it through Agent mode, and review the diff file by file plus the real test output before accepting.
lessons.expectedResult: Agent produces a change matching your acceptance criteria, reuses existing patterns rather than duplicating logic where one already exists, and you have real test output (not a claim) confirming it works before you commit.
commonMistakes: Giving a vague one-line task ('add validation') instead of a spec with acceptance criteria and constraints, leading to guessed scope.
Letting Agent run unsupervised through a long, ambiguous task instead of interrupting early when it heads the wrong way.
Accepting 'tests pass' as a claim without seeing the actual command output.
lessons.proTip: Model choice is also a cost lever — Auto is usually fine for routine, well-scoped tasks, but reserve a flagship model for architecture-sensitive or ambiguous work, since frontier models draw down your usage-credit pool faster.

lessons.title: Write Rules files that keep the Agent on your team's conventions
lessons.summary: Create scoped .cursor/rules/*.mdc files and an AGENTS.md so Cursor's Tab, Chat, and Agent consistently follow your project's real conventions instead of generic defaults.
lessons.goal: Set up a working .cursor/rules/ structure, plus an AGENTS.md if useful, that measurably changes Agent's output to match your project's actual conventions.
lessons.whyItMatters: Without standing instructions, Cursor's Agent falls back on generic patterns instead of your team's actual conventions — the library you've standardized on, the error-handling style you use, the folders that are off-limits. Rules files are how a team encodes that context once so it applies to every future task instead of being re-explained in every prompt, and legacy root .cursorrules files no longer work with Agent mode, so getting the modern format right matters.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A real project, and awareness of one or two conventions you keep having to repeat to Cursor manually — a state-management pattern, a naming convention, a 'don't touch this folder' rule.
steps: Create a `.cursor/rules/` folder at the project root if one doesn't exist.
Write one short rule file per concern rather than one giant file — e.g. `.cursor/rules/style.mdc` for general conventions.

Give each rule file YAML frontmatter: a `description`, and either `alwaysApply: true` for project-wide rules or a `globs` pattern to scope it (e.g. `globs: ["**/*.tsx"]` for React-specific guidance only).
Keep the body of each rule short and concrete — actual conventions and examples, not vague aspirations.
If the repo has (or should have) a root AGENTS.md, the cross-tool standard Cursor also reads, keep ambient 'how we code' context there and keep .mdc rules for Cursor-specific, scoped guidance.
Delete or migrate any legacy root `.cursorrules` file — Agent mode ignores it.
Test the rule: ask Agent to do a task that would normally violate the convention, and confirm it now follows the rule instead.
Revisit rules after a task where Agent got a convention wrong — that's a signal to add or sharpen a rule, not just correct it inline again.
lessons.prompt:
Example .cursor/rules/style.mdc:
---
description: Core project conventions for all code
alwaysApply: true
---
# Conventions
- Use named exports only, never default exports.
- All async functions must handle errors with our try/catch + logError() pattern (see src/lib/logging.ts) — never swallow errors silently.
- Do not add new npm dependencies without flagging it in your response first.

Example .cursor/rules/react-components.mdc:
---
description: React component conventions
globs: ["**/*.tsx"]
---
# React components
- Use function components with hooks only, never class components.
- Props types are defined inline with `interface Props`, not a separate types file, unless the type is shared across 3+ components.
- Co-locate a component's test file in the same folder as `Component.test.tsx`.
lessons.explanation: The `alwaysApply: true` frontmatter makes a rule ambient — applied to every Agent task regardless of which files are touched — while `globs` scopes a rule so React-specific guidance doesn't clutter unrelated backend edits with irrelevant context, keeping each task's effective instructions smaller and more precise. Splitting rules into short, focused files instead of one long document makes each one easier to keep accurate over time, and citing a real file (`src/lib/logging.ts`) instead of describing a pattern abstractly gives Agent something concrete to imitate rather than an adjective to interpret.
lessons.example: A team keeps getting default-exported components and swallowed errors from Agent-generated code. They add the style.mdc rule above with alwaysApply: true. The next time a developer asks Agent to add a new async data-fetching function, it automatically follows the try/catch + logError() pattern and uses a named export, without either convention being restated in the task prompt.
lessons.exercise: In your own project, identify one convention you've had to repeat to Cursor more than once. Write it as a short .cursor/rules/*.mdc file with proper frontmatter (alwaysApply or a scoped glob), then give Agent a task that would normally violate it and confirm the rule changes the output.
lessons.expectedResult: A .cursor/rules/ folder with at least one working rule file, and a task where Agent's output now follows the documented convention (named exports, error handling, whatever you targeted) without you restating it in the prompt.
commonMistakes: Writing one giant rules file with everything in it instead of short, focused files, making it hard to keep accurate.
Leaving a legacy root .cursorrules file in place, not realizing Agent mode ignores it entirely.
Writing rules as vague aspirations ('write clean code') instead of concrete, checkable conventions with a real file reference.
lessons.proTip: Use globs to scope expensive or noisy guidance (a long design-system rule) to only the file types it actually applies to — an alwaysApply rule that's too long adds irrelevant context (and cost) to every single task, even ones it has nothing to do with.

lessons.title: Debug a real failure in Cursor without accepting the first plausible fix
lessons.summary: Use Agent to reproduce, diagnose, and fix a failing test or bug with a verified root cause, and treat automated review comments as a second check, not the final word.
lessons.goal: Fix a real bug or failing test with a confirmed root cause and a minimal, verified diff, instead of accepting the first plausible-looking patch.
lessons.whyItMatters: An agent under pressure to make an error go away can take the fastest route — loosening an assertion, wrapping the problem in a try/catch, or patching the symptom instead of the cause. Cursor's ability to run your terminal and tests as part of the same session is exactly what lets you require reproduction and evidence before any fix, turning 'trust me' into 'confirmed.'
lessons.beforeYouStart: A real project with a currently failing test or a reproducible bug, and the full error output or stack trace — not a paraphrase.
steps: Open Agent and paste the complete error output and stack trace, not a summary of it.
Ask Agent to reproduce the failure by actually running the relevant command in the terminal, and confirm it sees the same error before proposing anything.
Ask for a root-cause hypothesis in plain language, citing the specific line or condition responsible, before any code changes.
Push back if the hypothesis isn't backed by something checkable in the code — ask what evidence supports it.
Once the hypothesis holds up, ask for the minimal fix — not a broader refactor mixed in.
Explicitly ask whether the fix touches any existing test, and if so, require a plain-language justification.
Rerun the full test suite (not just the one failing test) and review the complete output.
If an automated code-review pass (e.g. BugBot) is enabled on the project, treat any comment it raises on the fix as a second check, not the final word.
lessons.prompt:
Here is the exact failing output:

[PASTE FULL ERROR AND STACK TRACE]

First, reproduce this by running the actual command in the terminal and confirm you see the same failure — show me the command and its output. Then state your root-cause hypothesis in plain language, citing the specific line(s) responsible, and do not propose a fix yet. Once I confirm the hypothesis makes sense, implement the minimal fix — nothing else. Tell me explicitly if the fix requires changing any existing test, and justify why the old test's expectation was wrong if so. Finally, run the full test suite (not just this test) and show me the complete output.
lessons.explanation: Requiring Agent to actually reproduce the failure in the terminal, not just read the pasted trace, rules out a fix based on a misread of the error. Separating the root-cause hypothesis into its own checkpoint, before any code is touched, gives you a cheap moment to redirect ('that's not the actual cause, look at the caller instead') before wasted implementation effort. Explicitly asking whether an existing test changed surfaces the riskiest kind of 'fix': one that makes a failure disappear by redefining correctness rather than correcting the code.
lessons.example: A test fails with a TypeError when a null value reaches a date-formatting function. Agent reproduces it locally, runs the test command, and confirms the same failure. Its hypothesis: a recent change upstream removed a null check before calling the formatter. Rather than adding a defensive try/catch inside the formatter itself, it restores the check at the actual source, confirms no existing test needed modification, and reruns the full suite showing all tests passing.
lessons.exercise: Find or intentionally cause a failing test in a practice project. Run it through this reproduce-hypothesize-fix-rerun cycle using the prompt above, paying close attention to whether Agent ever proposes touching an existing test to make the failure disappear.
lessons.expectedResult: A confirmed root cause backed by a specific, checkable line or condition, a minimal fix addressing that cause, an honest answer on whether any existing test changed, and a full test suite rerun (not just the one test) showing everything passing.
commonMistakes: Pasting only the error message instead of the full stack trace, forcing Agent to guess at context it needs.
Accepting the first proposed fix without confirming the root-cause hypothesis first.
Letting a fix quietly weaken or skip the failing test instead of addressing the underlying code.
lessons.proTip: If BugBot or another automated review is enabled on the repo, don't treat its comments on your fix as mandatory or as noise by default — triage each one explicitly (fix, or reject with a one-line reason), the same discipline you'd apply to a human reviewer's comment.

lessons.title: Run background and cloud agents for bigger, parallel tasks
lessons.summary: Dispatch multiple independent, well-specified tasks to Cursor's background and cloud agents running in isolated VMs, and review results asynchronously instead of watching each one live.
lessons.goal: Safely run two or three independent tasks in parallel as background/cloud agents, and review the returned work asynchronously.
lessons.whyItMatters: Cursor's Cloud Agents run in isolated cloud VMs with their own terminal, browser, and desktop access, and can work across multiple repos, reporting back asynchronously — a real multiplier when you have several independent, well-bounded tasks instead of one. But unlike a live Agent session where you can interrupt mid-task, background and cloud agents run unsupervised, so ambiguity in the task compounds silently until you're looking at finished work. Knowing which tasks are safe to send there is what makes the parallelism a gain instead of a liability.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A Cursor plan with Cloud Agent access, at least one connected repository, and two or three genuinely independent, well-scoped tasks in mind that don't overlap the same files.
steps: Identify tasks that are independent of each other and don't touch the same files — background/cloud agents run in parallel, and overlapping edits create conflicts you'll have to resolve manually.
For each task, write a full spec exactly as you would for a supervised Agent session — goal, constraints, definition of done — since there's no one present to clarify a vague instruction mid-run.
Dispatch each task as a background or cloud agent rather than a live session you have to watch.
Let them run without babysitting — that's the point; check back once notified or after an appropriate interval.
Review each result as a finished diff (or pull request, if the agent opens one), not code-in-progress.
Pull any promising result down and run your own build/test suite locally before merging — don't trust a cloud environment's 'it passed' claim alone.
Reject or send back any task that drifted from spec, with a specific correction, rather than assuming small deviations are fine.
Reserve genuinely ambiguous or high-stakes work for a live, supervised Agent session instead of background/cloud dispatch.
lessons.prompt:
Background task 1: Add unit tests to src/utils/currency.ts covering the existing formatCurrency and parseCurrency functions, including edge cases (zero, negative, non-numeric input). Do not modify the functions themselves. Definition of done: new tests pass, existing tests unaffected.

Background task 2: Update all dependencies in package.json to their latest minor versions (not major). Do not touch major-version bumps. Run the full test suite after updating and report the output. Definition of done: `npm test` passes with no changes to test files.

Background task 3: Add JSDoc comments to every exported function in src/api/ describing parameters and return values, based only on how each function is actually used elsewhere in the codebase. Do not change any function's behavior. Definition of done: no code changes outside of comments.
lessons.explanation: Each spec above is deliberately narrow and self-contained — no ambiguity that would need a mid-task clarification, and no file overlap between the three tasks, so they're safe to run genuinely in parallel. The explicit 'do not modify the functions themselves' / 'do not touch major-version bumps' / 'do not change behavior' constraints matter more here than in a supervised session, because there's no live checkpoint to catch an agent quietly expanding scope on its own initiative.
lessons.example: A developer dispatches the three tasks above as background agents on a Friday afternoon: test coverage, a minor dependency bump, and documentation. By the next check-in, all three have finished. The test-coverage and documentation tasks are reviewed and merged directly. The dependency bump's test run shows one new failure; the developer sends it back with a note pointing at the specific package version that broke a test, rather than assuming the whole task should be redone.
lessons.exercise: Identify two or three genuinely independent, well-scoped tasks in your own project — tests, docs, a dependency update, a small isolated bugfix. Write each as a tight spec, dispatch them as background or cloud agents in parallel, and review each result as a finished diff before merging any of them.
lessons.expectedResult: Multiple tasks complete independently without file conflicts between them, each result matches its spec closely enough to review as a finished diff, and at least one task you dispatched required a targeted correction rather than a full redo — showing you're reviewing, not rubber-stamping.
commonMistakes: Dispatching tasks that touch overlapping files, creating merge conflicts between two 'independent' background agents.
Sending ambiguous or high-stakes work to an unsupervised background agent instead of a live, interruptible session.
Trusting a cloud agent's own report that tests passed without rerunning them yourself locally.
lessons.proTip: Background and cloud agent usage draws from the same usage-credit pool as your live Agent sessions — running several in parallel is a real productivity gain, but it's also a real cost lever, so reserve it for tasks where the parallelism is actually worth more than the credits spent.

lessons.title: Run a complete feature delivery workflow in Cursor, spec to merged PR
lessons.summary: Combine Rules-backed context, Agent implementation, verification, and review triage into one repeatable delivery pipeline from a written spec to a merged pull request.
lessons.goal: Take a real feature or fix from a written spec through Agent implementation, verification, and review to a merged pull request, with deliberate checkpoints at each stage.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every earlier lesson in this path is one piece of the workflow; this is the assembly. Professionals who get durable value from Cursor don't treat each Agent session as a one-off — they run the same repeatable pipeline every time, backed by Rules files that already encode team conventions, so quality doesn't depend on how careful they happened to feel that day.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A project with .cursor/rules/ set up (from the earlier lesson), a runnable test suite, and GitHub-based pull requests. Comfort with spec-writing, Agent checkpoints, and debugging discipline from earlier lessons in this path.
steps: Turn the task (ticket, bug report, feature request) into a full spec: goal, acceptance criteria, constraints, definition of done.
Confirm your Rules files already cover the relevant conventions — if the task exposes a convention that isn't documented yet, add it to a rule file before starting, not after.
Decide live Agent session or background/cloud dispatch based on how bounded and well-understood the task is.
Implement with checkpoints: review the plan or early direction, interrupt if it's heading the wrong way, review the diff file by file when done.
Require Agent to run the real build/test/lint commands and paste actual output — never accept a claim that it works.
Open the pull request with a description stating what changed and why, mapped to your acceptance criteria.
If automated review (e.g. BugBot) is enabled, triage every comment explicitly as fix or reject-with-reason.
Do a final personal read of the complete diff yourself, even if every earlier checkpoint looked clean.
Merge, then verify the change in the real running app — not just in test output.
Ask: did anything here reveal a convention Agent should already have known? If so, add it to Rules before moving to the next task.
lessons.prompt:
Ticket: [PASTE TICKET TITLE AND DESCRIPTION]

First, write this as a full spec — goal, acceptance criteria, constraints, definition of done — and show it to me before implementing anything.

Once I approve the spec: implement it, following the conventions in .cursor/rules/ and any AGENTS.md in this repo. Then run the full test suite, the build, and the linter, and paste the complete output of each. Tell me explicitly whether any existing test was modified and why. Finally, draft a pull request description stating exactly what changed and how it satisfies each acceptance criterion, so I can open the PR myself.
lessons.explanation: Chaining explicit checkpoints — spec approval, implementation grounded in your existing Rules, verified real output, then a PR description mapped to acceptance criteria — means no single stage carries all the responsibility for catching a problem. Pointing Agent at your existing .cursor/rules/ and AGENTS.md instead of restating conventions in the spec is what makes this pipeline actually repeatable and fast at the tenth task instead of just the first. Asking Agent to draft the PR description itself, tied to acceptance criteria, produces a reviewable artifact for the next person, not just a diff with no stated intent.
lessons.example: A support ticket describes a bug where discount codes stack incorrectly at checkout. A developer turns it into a spec with the exact expected calculation, runs it through a live Agent session referencing the project's existing pricing conventions in .cursor/rules/pricing.mdc, gets pasted test/build/lint output, opens a PR with an Agent-drafted description mapped to the ticket's acceptance criteria, triages two BugBot comments (one fixed, one rejected as an existing pattern used elsewhere), reads the 35-line diff herself, and merges. Afterward she adds one line to a rule file: 'discount stacking rules live in src/pricing/discounts.ts — check that file before touching pricing logic.'
lessons.exercise: Take one real ticket or task in your own project and run it through this entire pipeline: spec, Rules-grounded implementation, real verification output, PR description, review triage, and a final personal read of the diff before merging. Afterward, add one line to a Rules file capturing anything you had to explain that Agent should already have known.
lessons.expectedResult: A merged pull request whose description accurately reflects the change, backed by real verification output at each stage, every automated review comment explicitly triaged, and at least one concrete addition to your Rules files from what you learned.
commonMistakes: Skipping the final personal read of the full diff because every earlier automated checkpoint looked fine.
Re-explaining the same conventions in every spec instead of encoding them once in Rules files.
Never updating Rules/AGENTS.md after a delivery, so the same context has to be re-taught every time.
lessons.proTip: Treat your .cursor/rules/ folder as a living part of the codebase, reviewed in PRs like any other file — after each delivery, spend sixty seconds asking whether Agent got anything wrong that one more line in a rule file would have prevented. That habit compounds into meaningfully higher first-pass accuracy over time.
